pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–7; water can be solid (ice and snow) or liquid; snow is tiny frozen ice crystals; icebergs are huge floating ice chunks mostly hidden underwater; ice floats because it is lighter than the same amount of water.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS1 Y2 'Uses of everyday materials' and KS1 working-scientifically observation; foundational for Y4 'States of matter' (solid/liquid/gas, freezing/melting).
• Standards—US: NGSS 2-PS1-1/2-PS1-4 (materials and observable properties; reversible/irreversible heating changes); precursor to 5-PS1 particle ideas.
• Operational details: keep it observational and hands-on — ice is water gone hard; snow is made of countless tiny ice crystals (look at snowflakes/photos); melting and freezing swap solid and liquid back and forth. The headline wonder is the floating iceberg: only a small tip shows and most of the ice hides below the surface. Demonstrate by floating an ice cube in a clear cup and marking the waterline.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) sort pictures into 'ice/snow (hard)' vs 'water (runny)'; Tier B (6) predict and check that an ice cube floats and say most of it is underwater; Tier C (7) explain that snow is lots of tiny ice crystals and that ice floats because it is lighter than the water around it.
bestPractices: Use real materials — float ice cubes in clear water, mark the line, and let children SEE most of the cube sits below the surface
Connect to lived experience: freezing water into ice, watching ice melt on a warm hand, catching or looking closely at snowflakes
Introduce 'floats because it's lighter than water' simply and truthfully; avoid the false rule 'heavy things sink' (a huge iceberg is heavy yet floats)
Look at magnified snowflake images so 'snow = many tiny ice crystals' is concrete, not abstract
Use the iceberg tip-of-the-iceberg image to seed the idea that most is hidden — a powerful, memorable picture
keyRepresentations: Clear cup with a floating ice cube and a marked waterline showing the hidden underwater bulk
Magnified snowflake photographs revealing crystal shapes
Solid ↔ liquid picture pair (ice → puddle → refreeze)
Iceberg cross-section: small tip above, large mass below the surface line
commonMisconceptions: Ice is a different substance from water — it is the same water, just frozen solid
All heavy things sink, so a giant iceberg should sink — ice floats no matter how big because it is lighter than water
An iceberg is all above the water you can see — most of it is hidden underwater
Snow is like white sand or cotton — it is made of tiny frozen ice crystals
Melting destroys the water — melting just turns solid ice back into liquid water

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: water can be solid (ice and snow) or liquid; snow is made of countless tiny frozen ice crystals; icebergs are huge chunks of ice floating in the ocean with most of their bulk hidden underwater; and ice floats because frozen water is lighter than the same amount of liquid water (not because of size or weight). Teach it observationally and hands-on, building intuition through predict-then-check with real floating ice, and seed the memorable 'tip of the iceberg' picture. A screen model where a child tries to push a floating cube under is a strong scaffold, but real materials deliver the felt surprise most directly.

activities.title: Push the ice under — and watch it bob back
feedback: If the child predicts the big heavy ice will sink, show a big ice cube floating in a bowl: floating depends on being lighter than the SAME amount of water, not on how big or heavy it is.

If the child thinks the visible tip is the whole thing, let the cube float freely (do not push it) and look from the side through the clear cup — most of it sits below the surface. 'Tip of the iceberg' is literally true.
When the cube keeps bobbing up with its body hidden, point out that this is why icebergs float even though they are enormous.
activities.rationale: Reasoning before observing surfaces the common 'big/heavy things sink' intuition so the surprise of floating can correct it. A marked waterline makes the hidden underwater bulk concrete. Roughly nine-tenths of an iceberg's mass sits below the surface, so the tip is only a small part.
sourceClaims: Ice is less dense than liquid water so it floats, with roughly nine-tenths of an iceberg's mass below the surface
KS1 pupils observe and describe the properties of everyday materials including solids; Y4 develops states of matter and freezing/melting
learnerActions: Get a real ice cube or chunk and a clear cup or tub of water ready.
Before placing the ice in the water, PREDICT out loud whether the big, heavy ice will sink or float, and say WHY first.
Place it in the water and OBSERVE: it floats with only a small part sticking up.
Mark the waterline on the clear cup so you can see how much sits BELOW the surface versus the little tip above.
Try to push the ice all the way under and hold it there, then let go and watch it bob back up every time.
Say in your own words: most of the ice is hidden underwater, and it floats because ice is lighter than the same amount of water — not because of how big it is.
activities.intendedInsight: Ice floats because frozen water is lighter than the same amount of liquid water; size and weight do not decide it, and most of a floating chunk (like an iceberg) is hidden below the surface.

activities.title: Melt it, freeze it — same water
feedback: If the child treats ice or snow as a different substance, melt a little in the hand — it becomes water, the same stuff just frozen solid.
If the child thinks melting destroys the water, point out the puddle is still water; it can be refrozen back into ice.
Reinforce: solid and liquid swap back and forth; nothing is lost.
activities.rationale: Lived experience of melting on a warm hand makes the solid↔liquid change concrete and tackles the idea that ice/snow are separate from water. This connects to reversible heating/cooling changes.
sourceClaims: Students observe and describe properties of materials and reversible heating/cooling changes
KS1 pupils observe and describe the properties of everyday materials including solids; Y4 develops states of matter and freezing/melting
learnerActions: Hold a little ice or snow in a warm hand and watch it turn to water.
Talk about how the puddle is the SAME water, just no longer frozen.
Place liquid water somewhere cold (or imagine the freezer) and describe how it would turn back to solid ice.
Match a picture pair or sequence: ice → melting puddle → refrozen ice, saying which is solid and which is liquid each time.
activities.intendedInsight: Ice and snow are frozen water (solid); melting turns the solid back into liquid water, and freezing turns liquid back into solid — the water itself is not destroyed or changed into a different substance.

activities.title: What is snow made of?
feedback: If the child says snow is like cotton or sand, show magnified snowflake images so the crystal structure is visible.
If unsure snow is water, melt a pinch in the hand to show it turns to water.
activities.rationale: Magnified images make 'snow = many tiny ice crystals' concrete rather than abstract, and melting confirms it is frozen water.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils observe and describe the properties of everyday materials including solids; Y4 develops states of matter and freezing/melting
learnerActions: Look closely at real snowflakes, or at magnified snowflake photographs.
Describe the tiny crystal shapes you can see.
Explain that snow is not like white sand or cotton — it is made of countless tiny frozen ice crystals.
Hold a little snow in a warm hand and watch it melt to water, confirming it is frozen water too.
activities.intendedInsight: Snow is made of many tiny frozen ice crystals — it is frozen water, not a fluffy material like cotton or sand.

activities.title: The hidden iceberg (diagnostic discussion)
feedback: The friend is wrong on both counts: the iceberg floats because ice is lighter than the same amount of water, and the part poking up is only a small part while most is hidden below.
If the child judges by size/weight, revisit a big ice cube floating in a bowl.
If the child thinks the tip is the whole thing, let a cube float freely in a clear cup (without pushing it) and look from the side at how much is below.
activities.rationale: Both halves of the prompt target documented misconceptions ('big/heavy sinks' and 'the tip is the whole thing'), so a correct answer is hard to fake and reveals genuine understanding. Reason-before-observing exposes the underlying intuition.
sourceClaims: Ice is less dense than liquid water so it floats, with roughly nine-tenths of an iceberg's mass below the surface
learnerActions: Look at a picture or cross-section of a huge iceberg floating with a little poking up above the water.
Respond to a friend's claim: 'Something that big and heavy should sink — and what you see poking up is pretty much the whole thing.'
Say whether the friend is right that it should sink, and whether the bit above water is most of the iceberg or just a little — and explain how you know.
Discuss: Why does a giant iceberg float when a small pebble sinks — is it about size? If most of the iceberg is underwater, why might that be dangerous for a ship?
activities.intendedInsight: A huge, heavy iceberg floats because ice is lighter than the same amount of liquid water (size is irrelevant), and the visible tip is only a small part — most is hidden underwater.

constraints: Keep the work observational and hands-on with real materials where possible; a floating ice cube in a clear cup with a marked waterline is the core demonstration.
Avoid teaching the false rule 'heavy things sink' — a giant iceberg is heavy yet floats. State truthfully that floating depends on being lighter than the same amount of water.

Sorting pictures by state or 'does it float?' questions can check classification but do not themselves elicit hands-on manipulation or build the floating intuition; use them as a short companion to hands-on work.

A labelled iceberg cross-section and tap-to-reveal snowflake facts teach the pictures well but do not provide the felt surprise of pushing a real cube down and feeling it resist; treat them as supporting representations.

An optional screen model (clear tank, draggable cube that bobs back, a dashed below-surface line, a warmth slider to melt/refreeze where the water level barely changes, a magnifying-glass button to zoom a snowflake) can make the mechanism concrete; these are illustrative interaction examples, not required mechanisms.
A 2D cross-section conveys the tip-vs-hidden-mass idea clearly for this age; 3D is not required.
Phrase 'ice is lighter than water' as 'lighter than the same amount of water' so size does not get confused with the comparison.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all sources were previously marked verified:false and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The curriculum/standards sources (DfE, NGSS) and the NSIDC density/nine-tenths claim were all flagged verified:false in the source row; treat specific figures cautiously.

The explanation 'frozen water takes up more room, so it floats' (from the assessment correctAnswer) is a simplified causal link to density; for this age the phrasing 'ice is lighter than the same amount of water' is kept as the primary, truthful statement and the expansion-to-density mechanism is not pressed as a required explanation.

The original framing described dragging a cube and feeling it 'resist' — on-screen this is visual/behavioural rather than truly tactile; real materials are noted as giving the more direct felt experience.

No source directly supports the specific claim that snow is composed of tiny ice crystals; activity 3 leans on the general KS1 observe-and-describe claim and the melt-check, so the composition statement is taught as an observation rather than as a source-verified fact.

Activity 1's sourceClaims were trimmed to remove the NGSS reversible heating/cooling claim, which supports the melt/freeze principle (Activity 2) rather than the floating/density principle taught in Activity 1.

assess.poeTask: Give the child a large ice cube (or chunk) and a clear tub of water. Ask them to PREDICT, saying why first, whether the big heavy ice will sink or float, and how much will stick up. They place it and OBSERVE it floats with only a small part above the surface; ask them to push it under and watch it bob back. Then EXPLAIN: heavy things don't automatically sink — ice is lighter than water so it floats, and most of it hides below. The reason-before-observing exposes the 'big=sinks' intuition.
probeDeeper: Why does a giant iceberg float when a small pebble sinks — is it about size?
If most of the iceberg is underwater, why might that be dangerous for a ship?
What would happen to a handful of snow if you held it in a warm hand?
Is ice a completely different thing from water, or the same thing changed somehow?
assess.correctAnswer: The friend is wrong on both counts. A big heavy iceberg FLOATS because ice is lighter than the same amount of liquid water (frozen water takes up more room, so it floats) — size doesn't decide it. And the part poking up is only a SMALL part; MOST of the iceberg is hidden underwater. Ice and snow are just frozen water (solid), which can melt back to liquid.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Heavy/big things always sink' — judges floating by size or weight, not by comparison to water.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a big ice cube floating in a bowl; floating depends on being lighter than the SAME amount of water, not on how big it is.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — it's so big and heavy that it should really sink to the bottom.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts the iceberg should sink because it's huge and heavy.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'What you see is the whole iceberg' — unaware most is submerged.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Push a floating ice cube down and look from the side: most sits below the surface — 'tip of the iceberg' is literally true.
errorPatterns.distractor: The part you can see poking up is nearly the whole iceberg.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the visible tip is basically all of it; surprised there's far more below.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Ice isn't water / snow isn't water' — doesn't connect ice and snow to frozen water.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Melt a little snow/ice in the hand: it turns to water — same stuff, just frozen solid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats ice/snow as a different substance from water; unsure it melts back to water.

responseLevels.gap: Predicts the iceberg sinks and/or thinks the visible part is the whole thing.
responseLevels.full: Explains the iceberg floats because ice is lighter than the same amount of water (size irrelevant), that most of it is hidden below, and that ice/snow are frozen water that melts back.
responseLevels.partial: Knows ice floats OR that most is hidden, but can't explain floating by 'lighter than water' or holds only one of the two ideas.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a huge, heavy iceberg floating in the sea, with a little poking up above the water. A friend says 'something that big and heavy should sink — and what you see poking up is pretty much the whole thing.' Is your friend right that it should sink? And is the bit above the water most of the iceberg, or just a little of it — how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child running on 'big/heavy things sink' predicts it sinks and thinks what shows is all of it; a child with the concept says ice floats because it's lighter than water and that most of the berg is hidden below. Both halves of the prompt target documented misconceptions, so a right answer is hard to fake.
